title: How Others Think, Dissecting a Reddit Thread to Understand Sense-Making
author: Leadership Capability
summary: Using a real Reddit career-advice thread as a case study, this piece analyzes how sixty-plus strangers responded to a single dilemma, a person offered a higher-paying director role but worried their resume already read as 'job hopping,' to demonstrate how differently people interpret identical facts. Drawing on sociologist Erving Goffman's concept of framing, the author codes the responses into five distinct interpretive styles with rough percentages: dismissal (33%, flatly telling the poster they're overthinking it), relabelling (26%, reframing the same resume as valuable breadth), risk acknowledgement (12%, taking the concern seriously as calibrated), cynicism (12%, invoking a generalized belief about corporate disloyalty regardless of the poster's specifics), and deeper-meaning-seeking (13%, asking what's actually behind the question, including whether the poster needed Reddit's permission to make a senior-level call). The piece's sharpest insight is that the original poster wasn't operating from one frame but two competing ones simultaneously, 'I do a good job' against 'chasing money is bad', and it's precisely that unresolved tension between frames that produces anxiety and drives someone to crowdsource a decision from strangers. The piece closes with a practical reframe for readers' own stuck decisions: ask whether a dilemma is really two frames in conflict, and when someone else disagrees, ask what frame they're using rather than assuming the disagreement is about facts at all.
points: Codes sixty-plus real Reddit responses to a single career dilemma into five distinct framing styles with rough percentages (dismissal 33%, relabelling 26%, risk acknowledgement 12%, cynicism 12%, deeper-meaning-seeking 13%), turning an anecdotal thread into a structured case study of sense-making.

Applies Erving Goffman's concept of framing, the largely unconscious process of deciding 'what's actually going on here' before reasoning even begins, as the analytical lens for why identical facts produced radically different advice.

Identifies that the original poster held two competing frames simultaneously ('I do a good job, I deserve this' against 'chasing money is bad, what will others think'), arguing this unresolved tension, not missing information, is what produces decision anxiety.

Notes that the largest single response group (dismissal, ~33%) barely engaged with the poster's actual framing at all, suggesting the most common public response to a nuanced dilemma is to flatten it rather than examine it.

Converts the analysis into two transferable coaching questions: when stuck, ask whether you're holding two unreconciled frames at once; when someone disagrees with you, ask what frame they're using rather than assuming a factual disagreement.
quotes: The challenge with difficult decisions isn't usually uncertainty about the missing piece of information. The problem is anxiety, the emotional discomfort of not really knowing what the narrative actually is, caught between two or more frames that conflict in your head.

Erving Goffman, the sociologist who spent much of his career studying how people make sense of everyday situations, called this framing, the process of answering the question what's actually going on here, before any conscious reasoning even starts.

Dismissal: The largest group (!) ~33% of all responses. These commentators barely engaged with the author's framing at all, didn't acknowledge the hesitation, and offered flat judgement instead. 'Nobody cares. You are overthinking it,' was their verdict.
Going back to the thread, what's also worth noticing is that the author didn't bring just one frame. They brought two, and that's what triggers the emotional response, the anxiety and confusion.

When you feel caught in a dilemma, ask whether it's really two competing frames you haven't managed to reconcile. Is there a larger frame that could hold both at once, or a higher vantage point the situation looks different from?
